content: Endometriosis is a prevalent gynecological condition that affects many women of reproductive age globally. It is a significant cause of both chronic pain and infertility. The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) is frequently prescribed to alleviate pain associated with endometriosis, although the evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness, safety, and cost-efficiency of oral contraceptive preparations in managing painful symptoms linked to laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases and trial registries up to October 19, 2017. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women of reproductive age with surgically confirmed endometriosis were included. The primary outcome of interest was self-reported pain, specifically dysmenorrhea, at the end of treatment. Five trials involving a total of 612 women met the inclusion criteria, but only three trials (404 women) provided data suitable for analysis. The findings are as follows: 1. COCP versus Placebo: Two trials compared the COCP with a placebo. Both studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias. For self-reported pain (dysmenorrhea) at the end of treatment, the quality of evidence was rated as very low. This was due to imprecision (data from a single, small trial) and wide confidence intervals in the visual analogue scale data. Additionally, there was significant involvement of the pharmaceutical company funding the trials. Treatment with the COCP showed an improvement in self-reported pain compared to placebo. On the Dysmenorrhea verbal rating scale (0 to 3), the mean difference (MD) was -1.30 points (95% CI -1.84 to -0.76; 1 RCT, 96 women; very low-quality evidence). On the Dysmenorrhea visual analogue scale, the MD was -23.68 points (95% CI -28.75 to -18.62; 2 RCTs, 327 women; very low-quality evidence). There was also a reduction in menstrual pain from baseline to the end of treatment (MD 2.10 points, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.82; 1 RCT, 169 women; very low-quality evidence). 2. COCP versus Goserelin (a medical therapy): One small trial compared the COCP with goserelin. This study was also at high risk of bias due to lack of blinding and insufficient details regarding allocation concealment and randomization. For self-reported pain (dysmenorrhea) at the end of treatment, the quality of evidence ranged from low to very low. At the end of treatment, women in the goserelin group were amenorrheic, making direct comparisons between the groups for the primary outcome impossible. At six months' follow-up, there was no clear evidence of a difference between the COCP and goserelin groups in dysmenorrhea scores on a visual analogue scale (scale 1 to 10; MD -0.10, 95% CI -1.28 to 1.08; 1 RCT, 50 women; very low-quality evidence) or a verbal rating scale (scale 0 to 3; MD -0.10, 95% CI -0.99 to 0.79; 1 RCT, 50 women; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no clear evidence of a difference between the two groups in the complete absence of pain as measured by the visual analogue scale (risk ratio [RR] 0.36, 95% CI 0.02 to 8.43; 1 RCT, 50 women; very low-quality evidence) or the verbal rating scale (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.08; 1 RCT, 49 women; low-quality evidence). Conclusions: The evidence from two trials comparing the COCP with placebo is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about its effectiveness. The findings are limited by high risk of bias and cannot be generalized. Similarly, the evidence from one small trial comparing the COCP with goserelin is insufficient to make a judgment about its relative effectiveness. Only one comparison was possible, and the findings cannot be generalized. Further research is necessary to comprehensively evaluate the role of COCPs in managing pain-related symptoms of endometriosis. Future studies should also consider other formulations of combined hormonal contraception, such as the transdermal patch, vaginal ring, or combined injectable contraceptives, which were not addressed in this review.
